title: The Bronze Altar, the Courtyard, and the Accounts
summary: Bezalel makes the bronze-covered altar of burnt offering and the bronze basin, the latter from the mirrors of women who served at the tent's entrance. The linen-curtained courtyard is built around the tabernacle. The chapter closes with an inventory, compiled by the Levites under Ithamar, of the gold, silver, and bronze used, including the silver ransom paid by 603,550 men.
story: The construction has moved from the tent (chapter 36) to its golden furniture (chapter 37), and now it moves outward to the courtyard, where ordinary Israelites would bring their sacrifices. The bronze altar stands just inside the gate, the first thing a worshiper met. Everything about the tabernacle's layout teaches that no one reaches God's presence without passing the altar. The chapter then pauses to account for the materials, a sign that the building is nearly done. In chapter 39 the priests' garments are finished and the whole work is presented to Moses.
historical:
The altar was a hollow box of acacia wood plated with bronze, five cubits square and three high, about 7.5 feet square and 4.5 feet high, light enough to carry on poles and probably filled with earth or stones when set up (compare the earthen altar of 20:24-25). Altars with horns at the four corners are well known from ancient Israel. A large horned altar of dressed stones was found at Tel Beersheba in 1973, its blocks reused in a later wall, and smaller horned altars come from several other sites. In Israel's history a fugitive might seize the horns of the altar to claim sanctuary (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28).

The inventory's figures are internally consistent. A half shekel from each of 603,550 men comes to 301,775 shekels, which the text records as 100 talents and 1,775 shekels, so a talent here equals 3,000 shekels. By common estimates of the shekel's weight, that means roughly a ton of gold, well over three tons of silver, and more than two tons of bronze. The number of men matches the census of Numbers 1:46, taken about a month after the tabernacle was set up. The size of these numbers is a real historical question, discussed below. Ithamar, Aaron's youngest son, is named here as supervisor of the accounts; later he oversees two of the Levite clans who carry the tabernacle (Numbers 4:28, 33).
cultural:
The courtyard was a hundred cubits by fifty, about 150 by 75 feet, enclosed by linen curtains five cubits high, about 7.5 feet. That was high enough to block the view of anyone passing by. The only way in was a single gate on the east, twenty cubits wide, marked by an embroidered curtain in the same colors as the veil inside. The camp's ordinary life happened outside the white wall; inside, sacrifice and worship.

The basin was made from bronze mirrors. Mirrors in the ancient Near East were disks of polished bronze or copper, often with decorated handles, and they were prized possessions. The women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting are mentioned again only in 1 Samuel 2:22. The verb used of their service is the one used for military service and later for the Levites' duties (Numbers 4:23), but what these women did is not explained. Small inscribed stone weights marked beka, the half-shekel of verse 26, have been found in excavations in and around Jerusalem, a tangible trace of the measure used here.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 20 describe construction, following 27:1-19 and 30:18 but in a new order that moves from the altar at the center of the courtyard to the basin and then to the curtains that enclose it all. Verses 21 to 31 are an accounting report, the kind of record temple administrators kept, and they open with a heading: “This is the inventory for the tabernacle” (verse 21). Verses 22 and 23 look back and credit Bezalel and Oholiab by name, with Bezalel's full ancestry repeated, as if signing the finished work. Across chapters 35 to 38 the order of metals descends as the building moves outward: gold for the innermost furniture, silver for the foundations of the tent, bronze for the courtyard.

outline.t: The bronze altar of burnt offering
The bronze basin made from mirrors
The gold, silver, and bronze accounted for

doctrines.note: The altar of burnt offering stood between the gate and the tent. Every approach to God passed it. The tabernacle's silver foundations (verse 27) were cast from the ransom money of chapter 30, so the dwelling of God literally rested on the price of redemption.

The courtyard wall set a boundary between the common life of the camp and the holy ground around God's tent. Holiness in Israel was spatial: the nearer to the center, the holier the ground and the more restricted the access.
Every counted man paid the same half shekel, and the women gave their mirrors. The building belonged to the whole people, and the careful public accounting shows that the gifts were handled honestly.

words.note: Mizbeach, altar, from zavach, to slaughter or sacrifice, so literally a place of sacrifice. The bronze altar is sometimes called the altar of burnt offering to distinguish it from the golden altar of incense inside. It was the heart of Israel's sacrificial worship.

Tsava, to serve, the verb behind tsava'ot, hosts or armies, as in the LORD of Hosts. It describes the women who served at the entrance (verse 8) and elsewhere the Levites' service at the tent. The word suggests organized, disciplined duty.

Chatser, court or enclosure. The courtyard was the space where lay Israelites could come with their offerings. Later temples had several courts, and the psalms speak of longing for the courts of the LORD (Psalm 84:2, 10).

Beqa, a half shekel, from a verb meaning to split. Stone weights inscribed with this word have been found by archaeologists. It is the weight each counted man paid as a ransom for his life (30:13; 38:26).

christ: The tabernacle's layout made one path to God: through the single gate, past the altar and the basin, into the holy place. The New Testament speaks of Christ as the way into God's presence, and some of its language echoes this pattern, though the links are thematic rather than explicit. Jesus said, “I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved” (John 10:9), a saying about sheepfolds rather than the tabernacle, but one with the same shape. Hebrews says that the sacrifices of the old altar are fulfilled in the one sacrifice of Christ, and it adds, “We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat” (Hebrews 13:10). The silver of redemption in the foundations recalls Peter's words that believers were redeemed not with perishable things like silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19).

hard.q: Were there really 603,550 men of fighting age?
hard.a: The number, repeated in Numbers 1:46 and close to the round 600,000 of Exodus 12:37, implies a total population of two million or more. Many readers find that hard to square with a wilderness setting and with Egypt's records, which do not mention such a departure. There are several approaches. Some take the number at face value and see God's miraculous provision as sufficient explanation. Others argue that the Hebrew word eleph, usually thousand, can also mean a clan or a military unit, so that 603 units with 550 men, or a similar reading, gives a much smaller total; this view, developed by George Mendenhall in the 1950s and by others since, has to explain why the totals add up as thousands in the text as it stands. Others see the numbers as symbolic or as reflecting a later census applied back to the wilderness period. The internal consistency of verses 25 to 26 shows that, as the text stands, the writer means the numbers as thousands. Faithful readers differ on how to understand them, and the chapter's theological point does not depend on the answer.

questions: The women gave up their mirrors to make the basin where priests washed. What have you given up, or could you give up, that would serve others better?
No one could reach the tent without passing the altar. How does that shape the way you think about approaching God?
The accounts were recorded in public. Why does honesty in handling money matter so much in the community of faith?
